items.definition: A formal conversation with your manager about your work and how you are doing, usually held before a pay review.
items.example: I had a strong performance review, and I want to use it in my pay case.

items.definition: The range a role is paid within, with a minimum, a midpoint and a maximum.
items.example: My band goes from $1,400 to $1,900, and I am currently below the midpoint.

items.definition: The middle figure of a pay band, usually the point where an employee is expected to be fully competent.
items.example: I am about $120 below the midpoint for my band.

items.definition: A figure used to compare your pay with the market rate for the same role.
items.example: The benchmark for this role in Hanoi is around $1,750.

items.definition: Everything you receive from a job: salary, bonus, allowances and benefits, not only the monthly pay.
items.example: My total compensation is $1,650, including the transport allowance.

items.definition: A payment that depends on results, usually agreed at the start of the year.
items.example: I asked whether a higher bonus could work instead of a permanent increase.

items.definition: A single increase to pay that does not change your base salary.
items.example: They offered a one-off adjustment of $150 for this year.

items.definition: An increase given to bring pay in line with the market, framed as a fix rather than a reward.
items.example: The company called it a market correction, which is still a pay rise.

items.definition: A change of level within the same job, which usually comes with a pay band change.
items.example: They suggested a regrade to senior analyst.

items.definition: A payment made to an employee when a job ends, often calculated by years of service.
items.example: The package included three months of salary as severance.

items.definition: To respond to an offer with a different figure, as in a negotiation.
items.example: They offered $1,650, so I countered with $1,800.

items.definition: The first number of a negotiation, which every later number is measured against.
items.example: The seller opened at 120,000, and every figure after that was measured against it.

items.definition: A pressure tactic that claims the supply is limited, so that waiting looks like a loss.
items.example: The scarcity was easy to check: the shelf held six, not two.

items.definition: A pressure tactic that shortens the time available for checking and deciding.
items.example: The urgency was built to stop a phone call: sign tonight or the price changes.

items.definition: A pressure tactic that presents the decisions of other people as evidence for your own.
items.example: The offer came with social proof: nine out of ten customers chose the larger plan.

items.definition: The pressure to return a favour that the other side has given you.
items.example: The discount was the favour, and the renewal at the same price was the bill.

items.definition: The pull of a person you like, used to move the decision away from the terms.
items.example: The liking did not change the price, but it changed who got the last word.

items.definition: The pressure to act in line with what you have already agreed or done.
items.example: He had approved the budget, so the second approval came easier.

items.definition: The weight a loss carries compared with a gain of the same size.
items.example: The same 20,000 hurt as a loss and helped as a saving.

items.definition: The choice of words around a fact, which changes how the fact feels.
items.example: The framing changed nothing: 400 a month is the same money as 4,800 a year.

items.definition: A small, easy agreement that is used later as the reason for a much larger one.
items.example: The free trial was the foot in the door: the yearly contract came next.

items.definition: A large request made first, so that the smaller request looks reasonable.
items.example: The full package at 200,000 was the door in the face, and the single machine was the real order.

items.definition: The best deal you can make if the deal in front of you does not happen.
items.example: Before the meeting he wrote down his BATNA: the other supplier, the price and the date.

items.definition: The price above which the deal is worse than your best alternative.
items.example: He set his walk-away price the week before, and he did not move it in the room.

items.definition: Money, time or effort that has already been spent, and which is used as a reason to continue.
items.example: The sunk cost of the training was the argument for staying in the job.

items.definition: The capacity to stay in charge of your own reactions when the other person is difficult.
items.example: Her emotional maturity showed in the pause before she answered, not in the answer itself.

items.definition: The capacity to hold a reaction and choose when to act on it.
items.example: He used self-regulation to stay in the room instead of walking out.

items.definition: Reading what another person feels, and taking it seriously enough to act on it.
items.example: Her empathy showed in the question she asked instead of the advice she gave.

items.definition: The answer you owe for an act, to the people affected and to the law.
items.example: The mistake was hers, and the accountability was hers as well.

items.definition: The capacity to stay with a delay, a refusal or a mistake without making the other person pay for it.
items.example: Tolerance of frustration is what a good team leader buys with a calm answer on a Friday.

items.definition: The leaning towards acting before you have looked at what the act will do.
items.example: The message went out in impatience, and the impulsivity cost him the job.

items.definition: How strongly and how fast a person reacts to pressure; a tempo, not a character.
items.example: Her stress reactivity is high in meetings and low in front of a machine.

items.definition: The work of managing your own feelings and other people's feelings so that the situation keeps running.
items.example: Emotional labour is the invisible work of keeping a meeting calm.

items.definition: The feeling part of empathy: catching what the other person feels.
items.example: Affective empathy made her notice that the new engineer was frightened in the group.

items.definition: The thinking part of empathy: seeing the situation from the other person's side.
items.example: Cognitive empathy is what lets you guess that the deadline was the real problem.

items.definition: Stating your need, your limit or your disagreement without wrapping it in blame.
items.example: Assertiveness is saying the report is late and then saying what you need instead.

items.definition: The leaning that keeps the peace by not raising the issue at all.
items.example: Conflict avoidance kept the meeting pleasant and the problem on the table.

items.definition: A belief about a group that is applied to a person without looking at that person.
items.example: That sentence about men and women is a stereotype, and it settles nothing about the man in front of you.

items.definition: The part of the value ranges of two groups that lies on top of each other.
items.example: The overlap between the two groups is wide, so the average says very little about one person.

items.definition: The process of choosing a partner, from the first interest to the decision.
items.example: Mate selection was slow for her and quick for her brother.
